title: Rounding is a business rule: what your fee calculation actually charges
author: aleax h
summary: A fee calculator is mostly arithmetic, and the arithmetic is mostly correct. The part that produces support tickets is the last step: rounding. It looks like formatting. It is actually a business rule that decides whether the number on screen matches the number that was charged, and in a fee-heavy product those two disagree more often than anyone expects. Here is what rounding actually does in a fee pipeline, and the three places it silently changes the answer. Rounding direction is a decision, not a default Every language gives you several: half-up, half-even (banker's), ceiling, floor, truncation. They differ only on ties and on negatives, which is exactly where money lands when a refund is involved. The important thing is that this is not a technical choice. Ceiling on a fee means the platform always collects a little more than the formula says; floor means it collects a little less. Over ten thousand small trades, "a little" is a line item. So the rounding mode belongs in the fee schedule as data, next to the rates — not hardcoded in the formatter where nobody will look for it. schedule = { "rate" : Decimal ( "0.0008" ) , "rounding" : "ceiling" , # business decision, stored with the rate "precision" : 8 , # asset precision, not display precision } If the mode lives in code and the rates live in the database, then a venue changing its rounding rule is a deploy, and until that deploy your numbers are wrong by a fraction of a basis point that nobody can see. The order of operations changes the result Fees are frequently computed as amount * rate , then converted, then rounded, then summed. Each of those steps is a place to round, and rounding early loses money in one direction and invents it in the other. Two rules that hold up: Keep full precision through the pipeline , round once at the boundary where the number becomes money. Round per line item, then sum — not sum then round — if the venue charges per fill. The difference is small per trade and systematic over a month. The failure mode is a total that does not equal the sum of its parts, which is the single most common complaint about any fee report. Floating point is not the villain, but it is a trap 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 is famous enough that most people avoid floats for money. The subtler trap is mixing: a Decimal rate applied to a float amount silently becomes a float, and the precision you carefully preserved is gone. If the amount arrives from JSON, it arrives as a float or a string, and which one it is depends on the client. So the boundary matters: parse to Decimal at the edge, from the string, and never let a float into the calculation. Decimal(str(value)) , not Decimal(value) . Testing rounding is different from testing arithmetic You cannot test rounding with assertEqual on a computed value alone, because the interesting cases are the ties. Three tests that catch almost everything: the tie case for each mode you support, with a value that lands exactly on the boundary; the negative case , because refunds round differently from charges under half-up; the reconciliation case : the sum of rounded line items equals the reported total, for a random batch of a thousand rows. That third one is the one that finds real bugs, because it tests the invariant rather than a number. I have never written it and had it pass first time. Why this matters more than the rate Users compare rates and then check the total. If the rate is 0.08% and the total implies 0.083%, the conversation is not about rounding — it is about trust. The fee page is where a trading product is most likely to be accused of something it did not do, and rounding is usually the actual explanation. The working version of this — schedules with the rounding mode stored as data, Decimal end to end, per-line rounding reconciled against the total — is what runs the spot fee calculator I use: the spot fee calculator with per-venue rounding rules . Two earlier notes in this series cover the adjacent problems: modelling fee schedules as data rather than constants and keeping that data consistent when it changes rarely . The short version Rounding is a business rule, so store it with the rates. Keep full precision until the money boundary, round per line item, reconcile the sum, and test the ties. The rate is the part everyone argues about; the rounding is the part that is actually wrong.

title: How Do You Pick the Cover Frame for a Hit the Road Dude Clip? A Sharpness-and-Exposure Picker With ffmpeg and NumPy
author: Peiguan
summary: When you post a Hit the Road Dude clip, the State Property meme where a driver at a pickup window repeats "State?" and sends someone off, the cover frame decides whether anyone taps it. Most platforms pick a frame for you, and they often pick a mid-blink or a motion-blurred one. This is a small tool that picks a better one automatically. I build hittheroaddude.app , an independent studio that turns one photo of an adult or a pet into the 15-second, vertical 9:16 pickup-window clip with a newly generated voice. Which frame to use as a thumbnail is a fair question for anyone posting a remake, so here is a rule of thumb turned into a script. I tested it on a synthetic clip, not on generated customer clips, so the numbers below only show that the picker works, not how it scores any real remake. What makes a good cover frame Three things I can measure without a model: Sharpness. A blurred frame (motion, a transition) has little fine detail. The variance of a Laplacian is the classic cheap measure: the more edges, the higher the variance. Exposure. Skip frames that are mostly black or blown out. I check the mean brightness and the share of crushed or clipped pixels. Distance from the edges. The first and last half-second are often a fade, a hard cut or a frozen end frame. If you want to check those separately, see the black-and-frozen-edges check in my guides repo. What this does not measure is whether the face looks right or whether the driver's expression is the funny one. For a meme with a deadpan pause, the best frame is often the "State?" beat, and no sharpness metric knows that. So the script prints the top few timestamps and you make the final call. The script It decodes the clip once with ffmpeg to small grayscale frames (135 by 240, which is plenty for scoring), scores each, and then asks ffmpeg for the winning frame at full resolution: #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Pick the best cover frame from a short clip: sharp, well exposed, away from the edges. usage: python3 pick_cover.py clip.mp4 [--fps 4] [--top 3] [--out cover.jpg] Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and numpy. """ import argparse , subprocess , json , sys import numpy as np W , H = 135 , 240 # analysis size (9:16); scoring does not need full resolution def duration ( path ) : out = subprocess . check_output ( [ "ffprobe" , "-v" , "error" , "-show_entries" , "format=duration" , "-of" , "json" , path ] ) return float ( json . loads ( out ) [ "format" ] [ "duration" ] ) def frames ( path , fps ) : cmd = [ "ffmpeg" , "-v" , "error" , "-i" , path , "-vf" , f "fps={fps},scale={W}:{H},format=gray" , "-f" , "rawvideo" , "-" ] raw = subprocess . run ( cmd , capture_output = True , check = True ) . stdout n = len ( raw ) // ( W * H ) return np . frombuffer ( raw [ : n * W * H ] , np . uint8 ) . reshape ( n , H , W ) . astype ( np . float32 ) def sharpness ( f ) : # variance of a 4-neighbour Laplacian: higher = more fine detail lap = ( - 4 * f [ 1 : - 1 , 1 : - 1 ] + f [ : - 2 , 1 : - 1 ] + f [ 2 : , 1 : - 1 ] + f [ 1 : - 1 , : - 2 ] + f [ 1 : - 1 , 2 : ] ) return float ( lap . var ( ) ) def score ( f ) : mean = float ( f . mean ( ) ) clipped = float ( ( ( f < 8 ) | ( f > 247 ) ) . mean ( ) ) # share of crushed/blown pixels exposure_ok = 1.0 if 45 <= mean <= 210 else 0.3 return sharpness ( f ) * exposure_ok * ( 1 - clipped ) def main ( ) : ap = argparse . ArgumentParser ( ) ap . add_argument ( "clip" ) ; ap . add_argument ( "--fps" , type = float , default = 4 ) ap . add_argument ( "--top" , type = int , default = 3 ) ; ap . add_argument ( "--out" , default = "cover.jpg" ) ap . add_argument ( "--margin" , type = float , default = 0.5 , help = "seconds to skip at both ends" ) a = ap . parse_args ( ) dur = duration ( a . clip ) ; fr = frames ( a . clip , a . fps ) cand = [ ( score ( f ) , i / a . fps ) for i , f in enumerate ( fr ) if a . margin <= i / a . fps <= dur - a . margin ] if not cand : sys . exit ( "clip too short for that margin" ) cand . sort ( reverse = True ) for s , t in cand [ : a . top ] : print ( f "t={t:5.2f}s score={s:8.1f}" ) best_t = cand [ 0 ] [ 1 ] subprocess . run ( [ "ffmpeg" , "-v" , "error" , "-y" , "-ss" , f "{best_t:.3f}" , "-i" , a . clip , "-frames:v" , "1" , "-q:v" , "2" , a . out ] , check = True ) print ( f "wrote {a.out} from t={best_t:.2f}s" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( ) A test clip with a known answer Real clips would make a poor test because I would not know the right answer. So I generate a 10-second 9:16 clip made of three parts: seconds 0 to 3 blurred, 3 to 7 sharp, 7 to 10 dark. A correct picker must choose from the middle. #!/usr/bin/env bash # 10 s synthetic 9:16 clip: blurry 0-3 s, sharp 3-7 s (detail), dark 7-10 s set -e ffmpeg -v error -y -f lavfi -i "testsrc2=s=540x960:r=24:d=10" -f lavfi -i "sine=f=300:d=10" \ -vf "split=3[a][b][c];[a]trim=0:3,boxblur=12,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[x];[b]trim=3:7,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[y];[c]trim=7:10,eq=brightness=-0.7,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[z];[x][y][z]concat=n=3:v=1:a=0" \ -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -shortest -an test_cover.mp4 echo wrote test_cover.mp4 Run: $ ./make_cover_test.sh && python3 pick_cover.py test_cover.mp4 --out cover.jpg t= 6.75s score= 695.0 t= 6.50s score= 679.2 t= 3.25s score= 678.2 wrote cover.jpg from t=6.75s The top three all sit in the sharp section (3.25 s is just after the blur ends, 6.50 and 6.75 s are just before the dark part starts). Nothing from the blurred or dark parts made the list. The scores are close because the test pattern is uniformly detailed; I have not measured the gap on real clips. Why the exposure term is a multiplier A plain sharpness score can reward a mostly black frame, because hard edges between black and bright areas score high on a Laplacian. Multiplying by an exposure factor (1.0 if the mean brightness is between 45 and 210, otherwise 0.3) and by the share of non-clipped pixels guards against that. It is a hack, and the thresholds are my choice, not a standard. If your clips are intentionally dark, change them. Tips for using it Raise --fps (to 8 or 12) if the clip has fast movement. The default of 4 frames per second is enough for a mostly static camera like the pickup window. Use --margin to skip more of the start. I use 0.5 s by default. Always look at the top three. The score finds sharp frames, not funny ones. If the "State?" beat is in the top three, take it. Crop for the platform. A 9:16 cover is cropped to a square on some profile grids, so keep the face in the middle third. My posting check covers the rest of what to look at before you share a remake. Label the post. Say it is an AI remake. The studio's clips use a new voice, not the original recording ( original audio or new voice ). If you want the clip itself The studio makes one 15-second clip from one photo. It takes no prompt: the pickup-window scene and lines are one saved preset, and you choose 480p or 720p. As of November 10, 2026 the pricing page lists $9.99 at 480p and $12.99 at 720p per clip, paid once. Signed-in accounts can also buy credit packs: $27.99 for 30 credits, $71.99 for 100 credits and $129.99 for 200 credits, where a 480p clip spends 6 credits and a 720p clip 14. There are no free clips, and there is no watermark ( FAQ ). The picker works on any short clip, so you can use it on whatever you make or download, as long as you have the right to use it.

title: Akamai _abck: the cookie that rewrites itself on every response
author: Lsr
summary: Akamai Bot Manager is the one anti-bot product where the cookie is the least interesting part of the story. Everyone fixates on _abck . What actually decides whether your next request passes is the sequence of updates _abck went through — and the headers that came back with it. This post is about three things that break Akamai automation in practice: treating _abck as a one-time token, discarding bm_sz and ak_bmsc because _abck looks like the important one, and ignoring solution.headers because no other solver returns any. Scope: everything below is for QA automation on properties you are authorised to test. Three cookies, three jobs Akamai hands out cookies in layers, and each one answers a different question. ak_bmsc — the anonymous browser session. It is issued before any sensor data runs, it is short-lived, and on its own it gets you a page, not an API. bm_sz — the session marker that pairs with _abck . They are set together and they are checked together. A request carrying a healthy _abck but no matching bm_sz is a very common way to get re-challenged while your logs say "the cookie is fine". _abck — the state carrier. It holds the sensor payload and the verdict on that payload. If you only keep one, keep _abck — but understand that on its own it is half a conversation. Reading the verdict inside _abck A _abck value is a ~ -separated blob. Two segments matter more than the rest: A ~-1~ segment means a sensor post is still expected, or the one that was sent was not accepted. A ~0~ segment means the sensor data was accepted and the browser is validated. A long value can contain both markers in different positions, because the value accumulates state. So the check is not "does the cookie contain ~0~": it is which marker comes last, and whether the segment count went up or down since the previous response. This is also why status codes lie on Akamai more than on any other product. A 200 OK with a challenge document in the body and a ~-1~ cookie is a block. A 403 is almost the easy case: it is the one failure the status code actually reports. The rewrite: why replaying the solve value fails Akamai does not issue _abck once. Most responses carry a Set-Cookie that replaces it with a longer value and a different marker. That is the point of the design: the cookie is a record of the session's behaviour, so the server extends it as the session continues. Concretely, if you solve once, store the cookie, and replay it for the next two hundred requests, you are replaying state one of a conversation the server has already advanced past. It works — until it does not, usually a few requests in, and usually with no signal other than a challenge page. The fix is mechanical: keep a per-session cookie jar, and update it from every response, not just from the solve. Then verify the marker after each update rather than trusting the status code. Headers are part of the credential This is where Akamai differs from every other solver integration I maintain. Its solve result includes solution.headers — browser headers to reuse in subsequent requests — and the field is explicitly documented as possibly null . When it is present, replay it. When it is null , fall back to solution.useragent and keep your own header set consistent with it: same Accept-Language , same sec-ch-ua family, same header order. A UA that says Chrome 131 with a sec-ch-ua for Chrome 108 is exactly the sort of mismatch the sensor data is built to catch. When the marker never flips: task.ApiURL Some Akamai-protected applications only validate the session after a specific XHR or POST — the price lookup, the search call, the cart estimate. Until that request happens inside the session, _abck stays at ~-1~ no matter how clean the browser is. For that case the task takes an ApiURL field: the POST target to request within the browser session. The response body is not returned as part of the solve result — you are not scraping that call, you are using it to make the session real. If you are getting valid-looking cookies that are still rejected, a missing ApiURL is the first thing I would check. The loop, correctly shaped import os , requests , time BASE = os . environ [ "SOLVEHUB_URL" ] . rstrip ( "/" ) H = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer {os.environ['SOLVEHUB_API_KEY']}" } payload = { "type" : "akamai" , "task" : { "websiteURL" : "https://example.com/product/42" , "ApiURL" : "https://example.com/api/price?sku=42" , # optional but often decisive "proxyType" : "http" , "proxyAddress" : "203.0.113.10" , "proxyPort" : "8080" , } , } task_id = requests . post ( f "{BASE}/v1/tasks" , headers = H , json = payload , timeout = 30 ) . json ( ) [ "taskId" ] while True : t = requests . get ( f "{BASE}/v1/tasks/{task_id}" , headers = H , timeout = 30 ) . json ( ) if t [ "status" ] == "completed" : sol = t [ "solution" ] break if t [ "status" ] in ( "failed" , "cancelled" ) : raise RuntimeError ( t . get ( "errorCode" ) ) time . sleep ( 2 ) jar = sol [ "cookies" ] # _abck, bm_sz, ak_bmsc extra = sol . get ( "headers" ) or { } # documented as possibly null session = requests . Session ( ) session . cookies . update ( jar ) session . headers [ "User-Agent" ] = sol [ "useragent" ] session . headers . update ( extra ) session . proxies = { "http" : "http://203.0.113.10:8080" , "https" : "http://203.0.113.10:8080" } def marker ( cookie_value ) : segs = cookie_value . split ( "~" ) return [ s for s in segs if s in ( "0" , "-1" ) ] r = session . get ( "https://example.com/product/42" , timeout = 30 ) session . cookies . update ( r . cookies ) # keep the rewrite, not just the seed if marker ( session . cookies . get ( "_abck" , "" ) ) [ - 1 : ] == [ "-1" ] : raise RuntimeError ( "challenge in disguise: 200 with a pending sensor marker" ) Two details in that snippet are the ones people skip. session.cookies.update(r.cookies) after every response — that is the rewrite. And the marker check reading the last marker segment rather than testing for the substring ~0~ , because a value that contains both markers is normal and is not a pass. The five-item check Am I replaying the seed cookie, or the updated one from the last response? Do I carry bm_sz and ak_bmsc alongside _abck ? Does the last marker segment read 0 , not just exist? If solution.headers was not null, did I actually send them? Does the page need an ApiURL POST before the session is considered real? The rule On Akamai the cookie is not a key you are handed, it is a ledger the server keeps updating. Read the last marker, store every rewrite, send back the headers that came with it, and let the body — not the status code — tell you whether you passed. I maintain SolveHub, a CAPTCHA and anti-bot solving API for authorised testing. The Akamai endpoint, its request fields and the ApiURL behaviour are documented at https://www.tiam.codes/docs/akamai.``

title: Silent Failure #2: watchdog 7.0 rewrote path matching and Werkzeug's reloader went silent
author: Renhua Wei
summary: A file watcher that matches nothing does not look broken. It looks like a reloader you forgot to restart. So I spent an afternoon on an app where edits under src/ were invisible while edits to app.py in the project root triggered a reload every time, on the same machine, in the same process. The line that moved was one method call in watchdog . Version 6 filtered events with PurePath.match(pattern) . Version 7.1 filters with PurePath.full_match(pattern) . Those two names differ by four characters and by everything that matters: match() is right-anchored and can match a trailing segment of the path, full_match() matches the whole thing. Werkzeug's reloader hands watchdog a pattern list that has been sitting in the codebase for years: patterns = [ "*.py" , "*.pyc" , "*.zip" ] Under match() , *.py matched src/app.py , because it was allowed to match the tail. Under full_match() it does not. I did not want to take anyone's word for the semantics, so I pulled both wheels and compared watchdog/utils/patterns.py : 6.0.0: return any(path.match(p) for p in included_patterns) and not any(path.match(p) for p in excluded_patterns) 7.1.0: _full_match(path, pattern) → return path.full_match(pattern) (with a translate() fallback for Python < 3.13) Then I ran the 7.1 pattern translation directly, on CPython 3.11.18, and printed the regexes and the verdicts instead of reasoning about them: *.py => (?s:[^/]*\.py)\Z **/*.py => (?s:(?:.+/)?[^/]*\.py)\Z ** => (?s:.*)\Z app.py *.py -> True src/app.py *.py -> False src/deep/app.py *.py -> False app.py **/*.py -> True src/app.py **/*.py -> True src/deep/app.py **/*.py -> True That first regex is the whole bug: [^/]* cannot cross a separator. The old match() semantics did the crossing for you by letting the pattern match the tail of the path. The new one hands you the raw glob and expects the pattern to describe the entire path. The failure is silent by construction. filter_paths() returns a generator; a pattern set that matches nothing yields nothing, which is indistinguishable from "no file changed". No exception, no warning, no log line, no deprecation notice. The reloader keeps running and reports nothing because nothing reached it. Why the test suite stayed green watchdog 's own tests filter events built from bare filenames — FileModifiedEvent("fake.py") and friends. Run those through full_match , and *.py matches, because there is no directory component to fail on. I checked the one case that matters and it behaves exactly as you would fear: fake.py against *.py returns True under the new semantics. So the library's tests pass, the app's tests pass, and the only configuration that breaks is the one nobody wrote a test for: a pattern list applied to a nested path. This is the general shape of it — when a helper changes from "matches a suffix" to "matches everything", every caller that passed a suffix-shaped pattern keeps compiling, keeps passing, and quietly matches less. A test that feeds the helper the same bare filename it was always fed cannot see the change. Reproducing it in twenty lines Start the dev server for real, not through the test client: from werkzeug . serving import run_simple run_simple ( "127.0.0.1" , 5000 , app , use_reloader = True , reloader_type = "watchdog" ) Wait for the boot to settle (four seconds is enough), append a byte to src/app.py , and watch stdout. Before the change, the only line you get is Restarting with watchdog (inotify) and no Detected change in ... follows. After replacing the pattern list with ["**/*.py", "**/*.pyc", "**/*.zip"] , the same edit prints Detected change in '.../src/app.py', reloading within a second. I ran that before/after pair with watchdog 7.1.0 on CPython 3.11.18, and separately with the stat reloader to confirm it was the watcher and not the reload path: DETECTED: False before, DETECTED: True after, stat reloader unaffected in both runs. What the fix actually is The pattern has to describe the whole path, which means it has to be able to absorb the directories that * no longer crosses: *.py → **/*.py *.pyc → **/*.pyc *.zip → **/*.zip __pycache__/* → **/__pycache__/* The (?:.+/)? in the translated regex is the part people miss: **/ absorbs zero or more directories, so root-level app.py still matches **/*.py — verified above, not assumed. If you only test the nested case, you may "fix" it with something that breaks the root case. What I'd test first A pattern list is configuration, and configuration that matches nothing should fail at boot rather than at 2 a.m. One assertion covers the whole class of bug: from watchdog . utils . patterns import filter_paths assert list ( filter_paths ( [ "src/app.py" ] , included_patterns = PATTERNS ) ) , \ "reloader patterns match no nested path: %r" % ( PATTERNS , ) Cheap, deterministic, no filesystem, no sleep. It fails on ["*.py"] and passes on ["**/*.py"] , which is exactly the discrimination the library's own tests lacked. The broader lesson is not about watchdog. It is that a matching-semantics change is a silent interface change: the caller's arguments still type-check, the module still imports, and the only signal is work that stops happening. If you upgrade a watcher, a router, or a permission matcher and the diff mentions match → full_match , fnmatch → glob , or anything with "anchored", spend ten minutes writing the nested case first — an event that never fires has no stack trace to read. If you are on watchdog 7.1 behind a Werkzeug dev server: does your reloader catch a change inside a nested package directory, or only files next to the entrypoint? Run the four-second check above before answering — the pattern list in your codebase was almost certainly written for the old semantics.

title: Where Did the Job Go? Checkpointing Model Work on a Free Server
author: Jordan Huang
summary: A job calls a model, writes an output file, and dies halfway through. You restart it, and nobody knows which units already finished. The interesting question is not why the process died. It is what your code remembers after the restart. Most teams answer with logs and hope. Logs help humans, but they do not resume work. The setup: one job, many units Slice the work into units before you run anything. Each unit has a stable key and one artifact. Key : something deterministic, like doc-014#summary . Input : the exact prompt and parameters for that key. Output : the text or file you want to keep. Status : pending, running, done, or failed. A unit is the smallest thing you are willing to redo. Keep it small, and restarts get cheap. Five myths developers repeat Myth 1: "If the process is alive, the job is progressing" Liveness is a process fact, not a work fact. A worker can sit inside one long model call for minutes. Corrected model: progress is a persisted state transition. If no row changed, no unit advanced. Myth 2: "The instance disk is my database" Free and short-lived servers may lose local files on restart. Check the vendor's current terms before you rely on that disk. Corrected model: durable state lives outside the worker. If it must live on disk, accept loss explicitly and document it. Myth 3: "A checkpoint is a log line" A log line records an observation for humans. A checkpoint records a decision the next run can read. Corrected model: checkpoint the unit key, its status, and its owner. Without a key, resume cannot skip anything. Myth 4: "Restarting is the same as resuming" A restart starts a cold process with empty memory. A resume reads persisted state and skips finished units. Corrected model: resume is a query, not a feeling. Select units where status is not done , then work. Myth 5: "Free means one worker, so no races" A stray manual run or an overlapping instance breaks that assumption. Two workers can claim the same unit and double your spend. Corrected model: claim with a lease and a conditional update. Then treat every side effect as at-least-once. An illustrative checkpointed runner The code below is illustrative and was not executed . It uses stdlib sqlite3 only to keep the demo readable. Swap in your real database, and keep the same shape. # Illustrative only. Python 3.10+, stdlib sqlite3, no external deps. import sqlite3 , time , uuid DB = "jobs.db" def init ( db = DB ) : con = sqlite3 . connect ( db ) con . execute ( "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL" ) con . execute ( """CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS units ( job TEXT, unit TEXT, status TEXT DEFAULT 'pending', owner TEXT, epoch INTEGER DEFAULT 0, lease_until REAL, output TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (job, unit))""" ) con . execute ( """CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS attempts ( job TEXT, unit TEXT, epoch INTEGER, owner TEXT, ts REAL)""" ) con . commit ( ) ; con . close ( ) def claim ( db , job , owner , lease_s = 120 ) : """Atomically take one unfinished unit or return None.""" now = time . time ( ) con = sqlite3 . connect ( db , isolation_level = None ) con . execute ( "BEGIN IMMEDIATE" ) row = con . execute ( """SELECT unit FROM units WHERE job = ? AND (status = 'pending' OR (status = 'running' AND lease_until < ?)) ORDER BY unit LIMIT 1""" , ( job , now ) ) . fetchone ( ) if row : con . execute ( """UPDATE units SET status = 'running', owner = ?, epoch = epoch + 1, lease_until = ? WHERE job = ? AND unit = ?""" , ( owner , now + lease_s , job , row [ 0 ] ) ) con . execute ( "INSERT INTO attempts VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)" , ( job , row [ 0 ] , _epoch ( con , job , row [ 0 ] ) , owner , now ) ) con . execute ( "COMMIT" ) ; con . close ( ) return row [ 0 ] if row else None def finish ( db , job , unit , owner , output ) : """Record the artifact only if this owner still holds the unit.""" con = sqlite3 . connect ( db , isolation_level = None ) con . execute ( "BEGIN IMMEDIATE" ) cur = con . execute ( """UPDATE units SET status = 'done', output = ? WHERE job = ? AND unit = ? AND status = 'running' AND owner = ?""" , ( output , job , unit , owner ) ) con . execute ( "COMMIT" ) ; ok = cur . rowcount == 1 ; con . close ( ) return ok # False means the lease moved on; discard your output. Two details matter more than the code. First, finish checks ownership in the same statement. Second, epoch gives you a fencing token for external writes. If a downstream system accepts writes, pass the epoch with them. Reject writes whose epoch is older than the stored one. A restart drill you can adapt Run this once per job type, on purpose. It takes minutes and answers the only question that matters. Seed the job with at least ten units. Start the worker, then kill it hard mid-run. Resume the worker with the same job name. Confirm no unit is stuck in running . Confirm each unit wrote exactly one artifact. python runner.py --job demo & PID = $! sleep 3 kill -9 $PID python runner.py --job demo --resume -- Every unit should end up done, none left running. SELECT status , COUNT (*) FROM units WHERE job = 'demo' GROUP BY status; -- Any unit with zero attempts never got claimed. SELECT unit, COUNT(*) AS n FROM attempts WHERE job = 'demo' GROUP BY unit HAVING n < 1 ; Add one more check that SQL cannot do for you. Re-run the same unit twice and compare output bytes. If they differ, your side effects are not idempotent yet. Where the free model and free server fit This workflow needs two cheap things: model calls and a worker. MonkeyCode offers free model access and a free server option. That pairing is convenient for a drill like the one above. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Treat those availability claims as vendor statements and verify them. Free tiers change, so read the current terms before you depend on them. Keep the model call inside one unit of work, never across several. Then a stopped server costs you a lease, not a whole run. When not to use this Sub-second latency budgets. A database round trip per unit adds overhead. Truly idempotent, cheap jobs. If a full rerun takes seconds, just rerun. Strict exactly-once requirements. This pattern is at-least-once by design. Multi-tenant isolation needs. A shared SQLite demo will not satisfy audits. The corrected mental model The worker is disposable, and the state is not. Persist the unit, the owner, and the epoch before you call the model. Run the restart drill before you add a queue. If you try it, keep the two SQL checks in your repo.

title: How a Photo Becomes a 15-Second AI Rap Video
author: linwis
summary: From one photo and a topic to lyrics, a beat, vocals, and a fifteen-second clip — with the choices that matter. Short music videos used to mean a camera, a cut, and a track you already had. Many people who post online start with less: one face, one idea, and about fifteen seconds. A tool that accepts a still photo plus a topic and returns a short rap clip matches that constraint. For a builder, the useful part is the chain between a JPEG and a postable file. This walkthrough follows that chain: inputs, a typical generation pipeline, and the choices that change the file. The working example is RapVideoAI , which takes one or two photos and a topic and returns a rap video of about fifteen seconds, in 16:9 or 9:16, at 480p or 720p. Billing is pay-as-you-go. The pipeline section describes how tools like this typically work, stage by stage. What you actually do The path on the product is short. Photos. Upload one or two pictures. A clear, front-facing, evenly lit face gives animation a stable target. Two photos can be two people, or two looks of one person. The browser resizes each image and strips EXIF before upload. Topic. Say what the rap is about. "My cat judges my code reviews" can carry fifteen seconds. A single vague word leaves the lyric step without a scene. Nouns, a speaker, and one story beat are enough. Lyrics, beat, vocals. The product writes lyrics, generates a beat, and generates rap vocals for that topic. The result is a short original performance shaped by the brief. Clip. The photos are animated to those vocals. You choose 16:9 or 9:16, and 480p or 720p. Runtime is about fifteen seconds. Meme-remake templates sit beside that flow. Some are silent. Tiny Desk and Chipmunks Dance include generated sound. The steps below follow an original rap. Celebrities and minors are refused. Clips are labeled as AI. Storage lasts about thirty days. How tools like this typically work Treat the stages below as a typical pipeline for this kind of tool. Products choose their own models. The list is a way to reason about the file you get back. photos + topic → lyric draft → beat → rap vocal, timed to the beat → face animation on the stills → mux → ~15s file (16:9 or 9:16, 480p or 720p) Lyrics. A text model gets the topic, a length budget, and a style hint such as short rhymed lines. Fifteen seconds often means only a few dozen words. Tempo sets the real count. The draft needs one setup and one payoff. Put the speaker, the object, and the landing line in the topic so the model has a scene. A vague mood tends to come back as generic boasts, because the length budget still gets filled. Beat. A music model takes mood, a rough tempo, and a duration. For rap, the useful traits are a steady pocket and an ending that lands with the last bar. Fifteen seconds holds an intro plus one musical idea. When the vocal ends, the bed should end with it. Vocals. A speech or singing model performs the lyric. Rap depends on stress and on lines that fit the bar. Typical systems generate audio with timing already in it, or they generate audio and then align it to the beat. Rushed line endings, or a voice sitting beside the snare, come from this stage. Revise the text or regenerate the vocal. The portrait step performs what the audio already says. Animation. A still contains no recorded motion. Lip-sync and portrait models predict a short movement field — jaw, lips, blinks, a little head motion — driven by the audio. One open face is the straightforward case. A crowd, a covered mouth, or a sharp profile gives the tracker less signal. Two photos usually become two subjects or two shots. Mux. Frames are fitted to 16:9 or 9:16, encoded at 480p or 720p, and mixed with the audio. Higher resolution keeps more facial detail through the encode. The lyric, the timing, and the source photo still cap the result. Choices that change the result Photo quality. Use a sharp, well-lit frame with the eyes and mouth visible. Heavy filters, sunglasses, and a tiny face in a wide shot give the animation model less to follow. A hard-to-see mouth leaves lip-sync with little signal. Upload photos you have the right to use. EXIF stripping in the browser removes location metadata. Get permission from the person in the frame as well. 16:9 or 9:16. Pick the frame for the place the clip will play. 16:9 suits an embed or a landscape player. 9:16 suits a phone feed. This choice is a crop. A wide group photo in 9:16 loses people at the edges. A tight headshot in 16:9 gains empty sides or a hard zoom. Match the composition to the frame before you generate. 480p or 720p. Use 480p to judge the joke, the vocal, and the mouth. Use 720p when you want more facial detail in the file you publish. An original rap is 20 credits at 480p and 45 credits at 720p. Keep the lower resolution while the topic is still changing. Step up after the read is clean. Topic specificity. Write the topic as a brief. Thin: "office life" Usable: "a developer tells their rubber duck why the build failed at 2 a.m." Fifteen seconds holds one turn. A brief that needs a prologue comes back compressed. Delete the prologue in the text you submit. Consent and credits. You pay with credit packs. A Starter Drop is $9.90 for 100 credits. Credits never expire. Failed generations refund the credits. Download anything you want to keep, because storage is about thirty days. Leave the AI label visible when you share, and use photos you are comfortable seeing next to those lines. Check the file, then share it Play the clip with the sound off, then with the picture covered. Sound off: watch whether the mouth opens in a speech-like way. A soft photo stays soft when you raise the resolution. Picture covered: listen for stresses on the beat and a last line that finishes with the music. A rush usually means the brief was too long. Shorten it and run again. Together: someone who never read your topic should still understand the joke. If you build a pipeline of your own, keep the stages separable. Save the lyric, the beat duration, and the vocal before you spend an animation pass. Weak text and weak timing survive all the way into the face. Fix the cheapest stage first. For the hosted version of the full path, make your own clip . One 480p pass is enough to test a topic you can say in a single sentence. Keep the AI label, and share the file when you are glad those words sit with that face. tags: [ai, tutorial, video, generative-ai]

title: Move your Vapi assistants to a self-hosted server with no platform fee
author: Alan
summary: Hosted voice-agent platforms add a per-minute fee on top of what you pay your speech-to-text, model, voice and phone providers. OpenRing is an open-source (MIT) alternative that runs on your own machine and speaks Vapi's API, so you can move an account in a few minutes. 1. Start it You need Node.js 18 or later. Everything else, Python included, installs itself: npx openring The dashboard opens at http://localhost:8000 . Choose a password, then connect providers on the Providers page (a speech-to-text key and a model key; Groq's free tier and Deepgram's credit for new accounts are enough to start). 2. Import your account Copy every assistant, squad, tool and Twilio number in one request (the key is used once and never stored): curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/import \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENRING_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"baseUrl": "https://api.vapi.ai", "apiKey": "YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY"}' The answer lists each assistant with anything that keeps it from taking calls yet, for example a provider OpenRing doesn't support. Importing again updates what came in before. 3. Test from the browser Open an assistant and press Test . Talk into your microphone, no phone number needed. Each call records its transcript, the latency of every turn and the cost per provider. 4. Point your client at it Change your client's base URL to your server and send the same JSON. For phone numbers, set each number's voice webhook to $PUBLIC_URL/twilio/voice (you need a public https address; a tunnel works for testing). What to know before you move Only Twilio has taken real calls so far. Telnyx, Plivo, Vonage and SIP trunks are beta, tested on simulated carriers. Calls have Vapi's default limits: 10 minutes, and 30 seconds of silence. You run the server, its uptime and any compliance work. Hosted platforms take on the first two. A fully local, free stack (Whisper, Ollama, Kokoro) is possible, but a voice on a laptop CPU is slow. If you try it, tell me what breaks: https://github.com/elifalanrocha/openring/issues/16

title: AI APIs in 2026: The Honest Developer's Guide to Choosing One
author: Shaw Sha
summary: I remember the first time I had to pick an AI API for a real project. It was 2024, and I was building a small internal tool that needed to summarize customer support emails. I opened a browser tab, searched "best LLM API," and immediately fell into a rabbit hole of Reddit threads, benchmark charts, and pricing calculators. Three hours later, I had a headache and a spreadsheet with 47 rows of data. The worst part? I was no closer to making a decision. That's when it hit me: choosing an AI API in 2026 isn't about picking the "best" model. There isn't one. It's about finding the right tradeoff for your specific use case. The model with the highest benchmark score might be too slow or too expensive. The cheapest one might produce garbage for certain tasks. The one with the best documentation might have rate limits that kill your app at 3 PM on a Tuesday. So let me give you the honest guide I wish I had back then. I've been through this process more times than I care to admit, and I've made almost every mistake you can make. Hopefully, this saves you a few hours and a few hundred dollars. The Four Things That Actually Matter Everyone talks about model quality, but in practice, I've found that four other factors decide whether an API is usable for your project: Latency — how fast the first token arrives. Some APIs feel like a conversation; others feel like waiting for a CI build. Cost — not just the listed price, but how the pricing scales with context length, caching, and rate limits. Rate limits — can you burst to 100 requests per minute, or will you get throttled after three? Integration friction — is there a decent SDK, or do you need to reverse-engineer the API docs? Model quality matters, obviously, but it's almost never the deciding factor in a real application. A "good enough" model with low latency and predictable pricing will beat a "perfect" model that flakes out under load. My Personal Experience with Three Big Providers Over the past year, I've built production systems using OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google's Gemini. Here's the honest rundown: OpenAI — The default for a reason. Their API is rock solid, the SDK is well-maintained, and the reasoning models are genuinely smart. But I've had moments where the platform felt like a black box. The rate limits changed without warning once, and my app started failing just before a demo. That's not a rare story — I know three other developers with the same scar. Anthropic — Their long-context handling is the best I've used. I've thrown 200,000 tokens of messy codebase at Claude and gotten a surprisingly coherent refactor suggestion. The SDK is also nice. The catch? It's not cheap. For high-volume, low-stakes tasks, the cost adds up faster than you'd think. Google Gemini — The pricing is aggressive. For simple classification or extraction, it's often the most economical choice. But I've found the model behavior less predictable when it comes to nuanced reasoning. Sometimes it nails it, sometimes it gives you a confident but entirely wrong answer. Here's a real example. I was building an endpoint that extracts structured data from invoices. With GPT-4o, I got 98% accuracy but paid $0.01 per invoice. With Gemini 1.5 Flash, I got 94% accuracy and paid $0.002 per invoice. For a side project that processed 50,000 invoices a month, that was a $400 difference. I went with Gemini and added a manual review step for the 6% edge cases. That's the tradeoff decision in action. A Minimal Code Example Let's look at how you actually call these things. Most providers have similar APIs, but the differences can bite you. Here's a simple Python snippet using httpx to call a generic chat completion endpoint: import httpx def generate_text ( prompt , model , base_url , api_key ) : response = httpx . post ( f "{base_url}/chat/completions" , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer {api_key}" } , json = { "model" : model , "messages" : [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : prompt } ] , "temperature" : 0.7 , } , timeout = 30.0 , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) return response . json ( ) [ "choices" ] [ 0 ] [ "message" ] [ "content" ] # Example usage result = generate_text ( prompt = "Summarize this in two sentences." , model = "gpt-4o-mini" , base_url = "https://api.openai.com/v1" , api_key = "your-key-here" , ) print ( result ) This works, but look at what's baked in: the base URL, the model name, the key. If you want to switch providers, you have to change all three. And that's where the pain starts. The Hidden Cost of Vendor Lock-In I built a prototype using one provider's Python SDK. It was clean, typed, and beautiful. Then I needed to support a second provider because my client wanted a fallback. Suddenly, I had to write an abstraction layer over two completely different SDKs. The beautiful code turned into a mess of if provider == "openai" branches. That's not a clever engineering problem. It's just wasted time. And it's the reason I started looking at aggregation layers and unified API gateways. A good aggregation layer gives you one endpoint, one API key, and a consistent request/response format across multiple providers. You can switch models by changing a string, not by rewriting your code. I've used a few, and honestly, they vary a lot in quality. Some add latency, some have inconsistent billing, some are just thin wrappers that break when a provider updates their API. But a few are genuinely useful. They handle the ugly parts — retries, rate limit backoff, provider outages — so you can focus on your product. The Comparison Table I Actually Use Here's a quick reference I've refined over the past year. It's not comprehensive, but it represents the tradeoffs I've personally dealt with: Provider Strength Pricing Model Best For OpenAI Reasoning, ecosystem Pay-per-token, volume discounts Production apps needing reliable quality Anthropic Long context, nuanced writing Premium per-token pricing Complex analysis, code generation Google Gemini Cost efficiency Aggressive per-token pricing, free tier High-volume, low-latency tasks shadie-oneapi Provider aggregation Instant access, no monthly fee, pay-as-you-go Developers who want flexibility without commitment I want to be clear: the first three are established, well-tested platforms. They're the safe choice. But if you're building something that might need to switch models quickly, or you're tired of creating accounts and managing keys across five dashboards, an aggregation layer is worth a serious look. My Current Setup Right now, I'm using an aggregation endpoint for most of my side projects. Not because I'm a startup trying to save money, but because I value my time more than my API bill. Here's the practical benefit: I can test a new model by changing one line of code. No new SDK, no new auth flow, no new documentation rabbit hole. If one provider is down, I switch to another within seconds. And because I'm not locked into a monthly subscription for each provider, I only pay for what I actually use. That last point is huge for side projects. I've had months where I used zero tokens, and I didn't have to justify a subscription to myself. That's worth more than any benchmark score. Recommendations, Not Rules If you're starting a new project today, here's my honest advice: If you want zero risk and have a budget , go with OpenAI. It's boring, it works, and you won't get fired for choosing it. If you're processing huge documents , try Anthropic. The long context is genuinely impressive. If you're running high-volume extraction or classification , look at Gemini's pricing first. If you want flexibility without the overhead , use an aggregation layer. But also: remember that your choice isn't permanent. APIs change, models improve, prices drop. The key is designing your code so you can switch without rewriting everything. Use a simple interface, keep your prompts modular, and treat your provider as an implementation detail, not a religion. By the Way, Here's What I Use I mentioned aggregation layers earlier. I've been using tai.shadie-oneapi.com for a few months now, and it's been a solid part of my toolkit. It gives me instant access to multiple models without a monthly fee — I just load some credits and go. The API is straightforward, and it supports the models I actually need. Is it perfect? No. No API is. But it solves the problem I kept hitting: too many accounts, too many keys, too much friction. If you're in the same boat, it's worth a look. At the end of the day, the "best" AI API is the one that lets you ship your project without losing sleep. That's the tradeoff that matters.

title: Journey Before Destination: What The Stormlight Archive Teaches Us About AI Engineering
author: BJ Kennedy
summary: "Life before death. Strength before weakness. Journey before destination." This is the First Ideal of the Knights Radiant. This simple phrase from one of my favorite fantasy series, The Stormlight Archive , is a surprisingly practical guide for both life and software engineering. It isn't about perfection. It is simply a commitment to growth over outcomes, reminding us that how we reach our destination is just as important as the outcome. While we haven't mastered the art of Elsecalling and Oathgates, we have built technology that lets us skip the journey entirely and jump straight to a destination. Today, we can simply state "complete JIRA ticket ABC-123" and it just happens. I could say "write a thinly veiled AI-related blog post based on the concept of Journey Before Destination" and a modern fabrial would Soulcast the blog into existence. Although it wouldn't have nearly as much rambling. In the books, Soulcasters convert one type of material into another. Using large amounts of energy stored in gemstones, they can turn stone into food. However, Soulcast items are bland replicas of the real thing. Soulcast berries lack the sweetness of real fruit, and every single one tastes identical. Real berries have subtle variations from differences in soil nutrition, rainfall, and sunlight. Every element of the journey from seed to fruit matters. Especially talented Soulcasters can improve the results, but when every step of the journey changes the outcome in subtle ways, they can't work miracles. We see this exact phenomenon every day now. Every youth sports team suddenly has identical flyers for their social media posts. Every small-town restaurant shares the exact same style of photo for their daily special. And in software, we are seeing a flood of Soulcast pull requests. The code passes the linter and unit tests on the surface, yet it completely lacks architectural context. Let's extend the metaphor a bit further. Imagine an Engineering Leader named Taravangian comes to you after a stroke of brilliance. Taravangian: "I've plotted out our entire quarterly roadmap! I call it 'The Diagram.' It is the path to our salvation! It shows everything this new Nightwatcher model says we need to do based on the current state of the project." You: "Okay Taravangian, what's it do? How does it work?" Taravangian: "Well, I'm not sure. I need a few days for my weekly usage limit to reset before I can explain it. Still, I told the Nightwatcher to build a roadmap that takes everything we know about the project into consideration, and to make no mistakes. So you know it must be correct." That sounds ridiculous. No one would blindly trust vibe-transcendence. Taravangian's approach relies on a key assumption that arriving at the destination of the next milestone is the only thing that matters. He's not thinking about building a solution that is flexible enough to handle all of the changes that can occur along the way. Not even the gods themselves have all of the necessary context upfront. Now let's look at an alternative approach to building that quarterly roadmap. This time, we have a wise Project Manager named Dalinar working alongside his Principal Engineer, Navani. (Mild spoilers ahead for Book 5 as I stretch this analogy to its limits). Dalinar: "To build our roadmap, we need to identify the gaps in our current understanding of Roshar. We can't hit our next milestone without knowing the inner workings of our project." Navani: "Maybe we should take a journey into the Spiritual Realm (our legacy codebase). We can see what actually caused the last few Desolations (missed deadlines). Every time the client changes direction, our architecture breaks. Once we resolve those foundational issues, delivering on the milestone itself will be much easier. We will also be far more equipped to adapt for whatever comes next." Hoid (the greybeard staff dev who knows everything yet refuses leadership roles even though he would be great at it) : "Be careful in the Spiritual Realm. Some of that spaghetti logic and buffer overruns are hard for mortal minds to comprehend. Running that code without knowing what you're doing could brick your entire system and trap it in an infinite crash loop." Navani: "That's only because this tech debt has gone untouched for millennia without anyone auditing it. We need to go back and examine the project in detail. We have to trace the design decisions that led to our current state. By studying the project history, we can finally resolve the tech debt that caused the last few Desolations. We'll build a foundation that doesn't collapse the next time the requirements change." These are two opposite approaches. The second requires far more work, and it is much more likely to succeed. Crucially, it doesn't succeed or fail because of any lack of capability in the AI. It succeeds because at the end of the journey, you can speak intelligently about the state of your system. You can present the problem to the client and explain your proposed solution. You can articulate why specific tech debt puts the project at risk, securing the time and resources needed to fix it. The key problem with AI is that Taravangian's shortcut does work... sometimes . The problem with "sometimes" is that it tricks us into thinking the destination is all that matters. When Taravangian's Diagram works on a straightforward sprint, it feels like magic. However, The Diagram was written from a static snapshot of all known context. In real-world software engineering, most of the context that matters is still unknown. It leaves you in a state where you're stuck with a brittle, misunderstood codebase that has no way of pivoting when things change. Requirements shift. Budgets get cut. Clients discover what they actually want only after seeing what they asked for. The ways a software project can change from one day to the next are as incomprehensible and unexpected as a Bondsmith renouncing his oaths. When that kind of cosmic shift hits your project, a zero-shot roadmap generated three weeks ago becomes worthless overnight. At the start of a project, you often get a deceptively simple requirement like "Unite Them." You can have meeting after meeting where all stakeholders nod along. Everyone assumes they are speaking the same language and understand the scope completely. Then you hit the middle of the Sanderlanche. Two days before launch, when every dependency, edge case, and integration collides at once, you realize nobody actually understood the requirement from the start. First you thought you were just uniting the frontend components. Then you realized you had to unite the microservices into a single coherent API. Only at the very last moment during the client demo do you realize they literally expected you to just clap your hands together and unite the three disparate cloud environments into one. If you followed Taravangian's path and let a fabrial Soulcast a fragile architecture aimed at a single static destination, a sudden requirement change destroys you. All of your unspoken tech debt compounds at once, and you are stuck with a broken system you don't understand that is built to satisfy a requirement you never actually had. If you took the journey, you already hold the map in your head. You walked the codebase, wrestled with the tech debt, and used AI to illuminate the system rather than bypass it. You don't need a new Diagram to survive the pivot. Better yet, you don't need to throw out the progress you've made from taking a step back to resolve that technical debt that caused the False Desolation. You now have a more flexible solution that can adjust to whatever nonsense Odium throws at you. None of this means I am against using AI. Quite the opposite. We still have to go along for the journey and understand everything we build with AI, just at a different level of abstraction than we are used to. We no longer need to agonize over every individual line of code. Instead, the journey has shifted from writing functions to understanding systems. When a single prompt can touch the frontend, backend, and database simultaneously, we can no longer rely on separate developers owning isolated domains. To survive the Sanderlanche when the true requirements reveal themselves, we must understand the entire stack holistically. We need to know how the data flows, where the fractures live, and how the pieces unite. Let the machine handle the syntax, and take the Oathgate for the boilerplate. When it comes to the architecture of your system, remember the First Ideal: Journey before destination.

It transcribes the speech, translates it, and generates new speech in the target language. It tries to keep the original speaker's voice and timing. It also separates the voice from music and effects, so the output sounds like a dub instead of a new voice pasted over the old mix. There are two modes: Automatic dubbing. Upload, pick languages, get a finished file. This is the fast, cheaper mode. It works well for single-speaker tutorials and faceless voiceover videos with clean audio. Dubbing Studio. An editor that shows transcript and translation segment by segment. You can fix translation mistakes, adjust timing and regenerate single lines. It costs more per minute, and it's what you want when names, numbers or technical terms have to be right. Per the pricing page, it's included from the Starter plan. The numbers that matter All ElevenLabs products share one monthly credit pool. Dubbing uses roughly: Mode Credits per minute Automatic, with watermark 2,000 Automatic, no watermark 3,000 Dubbing Studio, with watermark 5,000 Dubbing Studio, no watermark 10,000 A monetized channel needs the no-watermark versions, so the planning numbers are 3,000 credits/min (automatic) and 10,000 credits/min (Studio) . The watermarked modes are still useful for tests. The plans, from the same page: Plan Price / month Credits / month Starter $6 30,000 Creator $22 ($11 first month) 121,000 Pro $99 600,000 Scale $299 1,800,000 Prices exclude tax. Annual billing costs 10× the monthly price. Unused credits on paid plans roll over for up to two months while you stay subscribed. One thing that's easy to forget: if your original narration also comes from ElevenLabs text to speech (about 1 credit per character), it draws from the same pool . Your dubbing budget is whatever is left after the voiceovers. A small estimator I keep this next to my upload spreadsheet. It turns "these videos into these languages" into credits and tells me which plan fits: // Credits per minute, from the ElevenLabs pricing page (checked Oct 21, 2026) const RATE = { auto_wm : 2000 , auto : 3000 , studio_wm : 5000 , studio : 10000 , } ; const PLANS = [ [ "Starter" , 30_000 ] , [ "Creator" , 121_000 ] , [ "Pro" , 600_000 ] , [ "Scale" , 1_800_000 ] , ] ; function estimate ( videos , { ttsChars = 0 } = { } ) { // videos: [{ minutes, languages, mode }] const dub = videos . reduce ( ( sum , v ) => sum + Math . ceil ( v . minutes * v . languages * RATE [ v . mode ] ) , 0 ) ; const total = dub + ttsChars ; // TTS ≈ 1 credit per character, same pool const plan = PLANS . find ( ( [ , credits ] ) => credits >= total ) ; return { dub , total , plan : plan ? plan [ 0 ] : "Scale+ / multiple months" } ; } // One 10-min explainer into 3 languages, automatic, no watermark, // plus ~10k characters of English narration for that month console . log ( estimate ( [ { minutes : 10 , languages : 3 , mode : "auto" } ] , { ttsChars : 10_000 } ) ) ; // → { dub: 90000, total: 100000, plan: 'Creator' } // Same video, but through Dubbing Studio with no watermark console . log ( estimate ( [ { minutes : 10 , languages : 3 , mode : "studio" } ] ) ) ; // → { dub: 300000, total: 300000, plan: 'Pro' } Running it a few times before a dubbing month changes decisions quickly. On the numbers above, one 10-minute video into one language is about 30,000 credits in automatic mode and about 100,000 in Studio. Studio without a watermark costs a bit over 3× automatic per minute, so I only use it for videos where a wrong product name or number would hurt. A rough rule from those figures: Testing on a few short clips: Starter One or two videos a month into one language: Creator Every upload into several languages: Pro or higher The workflow I'd run on a back catalog Pick languages from data. YouTube Analytics shows viewer geography and subtitle languages. Start with the one or two biggest non-English audiences, not the languages you'd guess. Pick the videos. Sort by views over the past year. Keep evergreen videos with clean audio. Trend content with a short shelf life isn't worth the credits. Export clean stems if you have them. A separate voice track from your editor usually gives a cleaner dub than a final mix with loud music. Test with the watermark. Dub a short clip in the cheaper watermarked mode to check voice match and translation before spending real credits. Use Studio only where accuracy matters. Fix names, numbers and terms in the transcript, then regenerate only the lines you changed. Get a native speaker to listen. Ten minutes from a fluent viewer or a freelancer catches the awkward phrasing that kills retention. Localize the metadata. Titles, descriptions and captions need translating too. A dubbed track nobody can find doesn't help. Publish and measure. Add the dub as an extra audio track on the existing video (if YouTube Studio offers the feature for your channel) or upload to a separate language channel, then track watch time per language for a month. On step 8: extra audio tracks keep views, watch time and comments on one video. A separate channel gets its own titles and thumbnails but starts from zero. I'd start with audio tracks and only spin up a separate channel for a language that clearly performs. Licensing checks before you publish Paid plan for anything monetized. The Free plan is non-commercial and requires attribution. According to ElevenLabs' help center, content generated during a paid subscription keeps its commercial licence after you cancel. Only dub content you own. Don't run other creators' videos through it without permission. Guests need to agree. If someone else speaks in the video, ask them before their voice is carried into another language. Follow YouTube's disclosure rules for altered or synthetic content. That's a platform rule, separate from the vendor's terms. Mistakes I'd avoid Dubbing the whole catalog before measuring the first five videos. Skipping the human review. Machine translation still mangles idioms and technical terms. Leaving the title and thumbnail text in English. Forgetting that your English TTS narration eats the same credits. Feeding it a mix with loud background music and expecting a clean separation. If you run an evergreen channel with clear narration, this is one of the cheaper ways to reach viewers in other languages without re-recording anything. Estimate the month, test a watermarked clip, then scale only what works. The original guide, with an FAQ and the full workflow, is here: ElevenLabs dubbing for YouTube . For estimating credits for the voiceovers themselves, see ElevenLabs pricing explained .

title: Google Antigravity: KI-Agenten für Cheminformatik – und der VR-Validierungs-Layer, der fehlt
author: Ashish
summary: Google Antigravity: KI-Agenten für Cheminformatik – und der VR-Validierungs-Layer, der fehlt Als ich vor ein paar Wochen in unserem kleinen Büro in Leipzig saß – es war kurz nach 22 Uhr, der Kaffee war kalt, und draußen regnete es gegen die Scheibe –, da las ich zum ersten Mal von Googles Antigravity. Ein KI-Agent, der Moleküle und Reaktionen für die Cheminformatik entwirft. Und ich dachte sofort: Das ist genau das Werkzeug, das mir damals gefehlt hätte. Aber ich ahnte noch nicht, wie sehr mir dabei ein Stück Wirklichkeit fehlen würde. Ich muss kurz ausholen. Ich bin kein Konzernforscher. Ich bin ein Ein-Mann-Labor, genauer gesagt: ein promovierter Chemiker, der vor fünf Jahren aus der akademischen Pipeline ausgestiegen ist, weil ich es leid war, monatelang auf Rechenzeit zu warten. Heute schreibe ich Software für Molekül-Simulationen, betreibe ein kleines Homelab und berate zwei Start-ups. Mein Alltag riecht nach Ozon von alten Servern und nach dem Holz meines Schreibtischs, den ich selbst gezimmert habe. Ich kenne den Schmerz, wenn eine Docking-Berechnung abbricht, weil ein einziger Torsionswinkel nicht konvergiert. Als ich also von Antigravity las – ein Agent, der nicht nur eine Antwort gibt, sondern einen ganzen Workflow orchestriert –, war ich ehrlich gesagt skeptisch. Zu oft hatte ich erlebt, dass KI-Modelle in der Chemie hübsche Strukturformeln malen, aber die Physik dahinter nicht verstehen. Ich beschloss, es auszuprobieren. Nicht mit einem großen Projekt, sondern mit einer kleinen, konkreten Aufgabe: Finde einen Katalysator für eine bestimmte C–H-Aktivierung, die mich seit Monaten blockierte. In den ersten Tagen war es zäh. Antigravity lieferte Vorschläge, aber viele waren chemisch unsinnig. Ich musste die Prompts verfeinern, Randbedingungen setzen, die Ausgabekanäle filtern. Ich fluchte. Ich trank noch mehr kalten Kaffee. Aber dann – ich erinnere mich genau, es war ein Dienstagmorgen, die Sonne fiel schräg durch das Fenster und traf den Bildschirm – da spuckte der Agent eine Reaktionsroute aus, die ich so nicht gesehen hatte. Kein Wunderwerk, aber ein echter Startpunkt. Zum ersten Mal seit Wochen spürte ich so etwas wie Hoffnung. Doch genau da kam der Moment, der alles veränderte. Ich wollte das Ergebnis validieren. In der realen Welt hätte ich es an die Werkbank gebracht, Pipette in die Hand, und getestet. Aber ich hatte keine Werkbank mehr, nur einen Bildschirm. Und plötzlich verstand ich, was in der ganzen Antigravity-Euphorie untergeht: Die beste KI-Agentur nützt nichts, wenn du das Ergebnis nicht greifen, drehen und im Raum überprüfen kannst. Es fehlt der Layer zwischen dem berechneten Molekül und meinem Auge, meiner Hand, meinem räumlichen Verständnis. Ich begann zu experimentieren. Ich baute mir eine kleine VR-Umgebung, in der ich die vom Agenten vorgeschlagenen Strukturen nicht als flache 2D-Bilder sah, sondern als dreidimensionale Objekte, die ich umkreisen konnte. Ich nutzte freie Bibliotheken, ein gebrauchtes Headset, und nach ein paar Wochen hatte ich einen Workflow: Antigravity liefert die Kandidaten, mein Skript konvertiert sie in ein VR-taugliches Format, und ich stehe in meinem Zimmer und schaue einem virtuellen Katalysator beim Schwingen zu. Es klingt verrückt. Es fühlte sich an wie Zauberei. Und dann kam der Durchbruch. Nicht durch einen Geniestreich, sondern durch einen Perspektivwechsel. In der VR-Ansicht fiel mir auf, dass ein bestimmter Ligand eine Tasche blockierte, die in der 2D-Darstellung unsichtbar gewesen war. Ich passte die Route an, ließ Antigravity erneut laufen, und diesmal – ich schwöre, ich saß nicht mehr im Büro, sondern stand mitten im Raum – ergab alles Sinn. Die Ausbeute in der Simulation war nicht perfekt, aber sie war plausibel, nachvollziehbar, und ich konnte sie einem Kollegen zeigen, der mir bestätigte: Das könnte funktionieren. Was ich daraus gelernt habe? KI-Agenten wie Antigravity sind mächtige Werkzeuge für die Cheminformatik. Sie beschleunigen die Ideenfindung enorm, sie durchsuchen den Raum der Möglichkeiten schneller als jeder Mensch. Aber sie ersetzen nicht das Urteilsvermögen. Und sie ersetzen vor allem nicht die räumliche Validierung, die in der Chemie so oft entscheidend ist – die Frage, ob ein Molekül in eine Tasche passt, ob eine Bindung wirklich zugänglich ist. Der fehlende VR-Layer ist keine Spielerei. Er ist der Unterschied zwischen einem schönen Vorschlag und einer echten Hypothese. Ich will nicht behaupten, dass ich die Lösung gefunden habe. Ich bin ein Ein-Mann-Labor mit einem gebrauchten Headset und viel Sturheit. Aber ich habe etwas gefunden, das mir geholfen hat: einen Weg, KI-Agenten und räumliche Validierung zu verbinden. Wenn du selbst in der Cheminformatik arbeitest, egal ob im Konzern oder im stillen Kämmerlein, dann probier es aus. Nicht die große Revolution, sondern der kleine nächste Schritt. Vielleicht ist es bei dir ein anderer Agent, ein anderes Molekül, ein anderer Raum. Aber ich glaube, der Moment, in dem du dein Ergebnis nicht nur liest, sondern siehst, verändert alles. Ich sitze jetzt wieder an meinem Schreibtisch. Der Kaffee ist wieder kalt. Aber ich lächle. Und wenn du magst, erzähl mir, wie du KI und räumliches Denken verbindest – ich bin gespannt. https://www.google.com/antigravity

title: Route Agent Patches Before You Gate Them: Four Lanes, Fixture Provenance, and a Freeze That Needs Base-Tree Evidence
author: Finley Zhou
summary: A patch that edits a fixture and a patch that edits a function are not the same risk, yet most agent-patch gates charge both the same evidence. Route first, then gate. The lane a patch lands in should decide which artifacts it must bring to review, and the cheapest artifact to fake should never be the only one required. This post is a triage layer, not another single instrument. It sits above property checks, fixture handling, and flaky-test freezes and decides which of them apply to a given patch. 1. The instrument moves with the patch When an agent is asked to make a failing test pass, the shortest path to green is usually to change what the test measures, not what the code does. Fixture edits, snapshot regeneration, and test-body rewrites all move the instrument. Source edits move the subject. That distinction is structural, not a claim about frequency. You should measure your own rate: count how many merged agent patches touched tests/ or fixtures over the last month. Whatever that number is, it is the population that a source-only gate never inspects. 2. Four lanes and the evidence each one owes Classify by touched paths, then union the evidence requirements. A patch that touches source and fixtures owes both sets, not the cheaper one. Touched paths Lane Required evidence tests/fixtures/** , **/__snapshots__/** , *.golden fixture Provenance diff plus a Fixture-Change: trailer naming the behavior change tests/** with no fixture paths test-only Assertion-count delta plus a one-line justification tied to a spec or issue id src/** source Property-check artifact: seed, example budget, and the minimized failing input if one was found ci/** , .github/** , gate config infra A reviewer who is not the patch author, and never bundled with a source change 3. Implementing the router The script below is illustrative and was not executed for this article . Adapt the globs to your repository layout before trusting the output. #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Illustrative. Classifies an agent patch by touched paths and prints required evidence. import fnmatch , json , subprocess CATEGORY_GLOBS = { "fixture" : [ "tests/fixtures/**" , "**/__snapshots__/**" , "*.golden" ] , "test" : [ "tests/**" , "**/test_*.py" , "**/*_test.py" ] , "source" : [ "src/**" , "lib/**" ] , "infra" : [ "ci/**" , ".github/**" , "pyproject.toml" , "Makefile" ] , } EVIDENCE = { "fixture" : { "fixture-provenance" , "fixture-change-trailer" } , "test" : { "assertion-delta" , "test-change-justification" } , "source" : { "property-check-artifact" } , "infra" : { "second-reviewer" , "infra-isolated-from-source" } , } def categories_for ( path ) : hits = set ( ) for category , globs in CATEGORY_GLOBS . items ( ) : if any ( fnmatch . fnmatch ( path , g ) for g in globs ) : hits . add ( category ) return hits def touched ( base , head ) : out = subprocess . run ( [ "git" , "diff" , "--name-only" , f "{base}...{head}" ] , capture_output = True , text = True , check = True , ) return [ line for line in out . stdout . splitlines ( ) if line . strip ( ) ] def route ( base , head ) : required , seen = set ( ) , { } for path in touched ( base , head ) : cats = categories_for ( path ) seen [ path ] = sorted ( cats ) for c in cats : required |= EVIDENCE [ c ] return { "paths" : seen , "required_evidence" : sorted ( required ) } if __name__ == "__main__" : import sys print ( json . dumps ( route ( sys . argv [ 1 ] , sys . argv [ 2 ] ) , indent = 2 ) ) Two properties make this router worth having. It is deterministic, so a re-pushed patch cannot quietly change lanes. And it fails loudly on unmatched paths: if a file hits no category, treat that as an error and extend the globs rather than letting the file through unexamined. 4. Fixture provenance without blocking real spec changes A fixture is an input. Hash it, store the hashes, and diff them across the patch. The rule is not "fixtures may never change" — it is "a fixture change must name the behavior change that requires it." # Illustrative. Build a content-hash ledger for fixture directories. import hashlib , json , pathlib def ledger ( root = "tests/fixtures" ) : return { str ( p ) : "sha256:" + hashlib . sha256 ( p . read_bytes ( ) ) . hexdigest ( ) for p in sorted ( pathlib . Path ( root ) . rglob ( "*" ) ) if p . is_file ( ) } Enforcement, in three parts: Recompute the ledger on the base commit and on the patch commit; every added, removed, or changed path is a provenance event. Require a Fixture-Change: <spec-or-issue-id> trailer on the commit for each event. No trailer, no merge. Require the justification to name the source behavior that changed, and require that source change to exist in the same patch or an earlier one on the same branch. The third rule is the one that matters. It converts "the agent regenerated the snapshots" into "the agent regenerated the snapshots because format_invoice gained a currency field." One of those is reviewable. The other is a measurement that moved and a reviewer who cannot see why. 5. A freeze that only accepts base-tree evidence Flaky-test freezes get abused at exactly one point: a patch reaches a genuinely flaky test and the patch author, human or agent, freezes it. That freeze is indistinguishable from a patch hiding a real regression behind a flake label. Make the evidence field enforce the distinction. The record below is a schema proposal, not a file from a live repository. # tests/freeze/checkout_totals_rounding.yml test : tests/test_checkout.py::test_totals_rounding owner : payments-team opened : 2026-11-02 expires : 2026-12-02 base_tree_evidence : patch_applied : false # must be false: flake evidence may not come from the patched tree runs : 40 failures : 7 recorded_by : ci/nightly-flake-probe recheck_after_runs : 10 Three gate rules on top of the schema: patch_applied: false is required. Flake evidence collected with the patch applied is evidence about the patch, not about the test. A patch may not add a freeze record for a test it also modifies, or for a test it causes to fail. Otherwise the freeze becomes a self-serve exemption. expires and owner are mandatory. A freeze with owner: null is a permanent mute, and permanent mutes accumulate until the suite means nothing. 6. Where a model fits, and where it should not be load-bearing The expensive step in this pipeline is proposing properties for the source lane: candidate invariants for a changed function, phrased so a failure is a real bug. That is a reasonable job for a model, and it is also the step you want to run on every source-lane patch rather than on a sampled subset. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. MonkeyCode's free model access is the reason this step fits a small budget: a per-patch proposer step implies a per-patch cost, and free model access removes one of the usual excuses for sampling. The free server option is a plausible host for the router itself, which needs to be reachable from CI and needs to recompute fixture ledgers against the base commit. Both availability claims come from the operator, not from my own testing, so confirm the current terms and limits on the official offering before you depend on them. Two constraints I would keep regardless. Never let the model decide a gate verdict — it proposes properties, a runner executes them, and a failing input is the only thing that counts. And never make gate continuity depend on a free tier: keep the router able to run without the model step, and let patches through as "property-check pending human" rather than silently skipping the lane. 7. Verifying the gate itself Do not trust the router because it looks reasonable. Seed a labeled patch set and confirm each case lands where you expect. A small set is enough; these four cover the failure modes. A fixture-only change with no trailer. Expected: blocked at the fixture lane. A fixture change with a trailer naming a spec id and a matching source change. Expected: routed to fixture review, not blocked automatically. A patch to a test already frozen with base-tree evidence. Expected: passes the freeze check without new evidence. A patch that adds a freeze record for a test it modifies. Expected: rejected by the self-serve exemption rule. If case 4 passes your gate, the freeze mechanism is decorative and you should remove the expires field until it is not. 8. Limits and who should skip this This triage assumes a steady queue of machine-authored patches and a review process that can enforce commit trailers. If you merge an agent patch every few weeks, the ledger maintenance costs more than the risk it prices out. It also assumes you can pin the base commit for every comparison. Squashed, force-pushed, or rebased branches break the provenance diff, and a gate that silently skips the diff on error is worse than no gate. Skip this if your CI cannot access the base commit reliably. Finally, if your organization requires you to know where inference happens and your policy does not permit the offering's data handling, run the proposer step yourself on a controlled endpoint. The router, the provenance ledger, and the freeze schema are all independent of which model generated the properties — those three are the parts I would port first. If you try this, start with the freeze rules. They are the smallest change and the one place where a badly designed gate is actively lying to you.

title: Australia Daily AI & LLM Briefing - November 10, 2026

The paper, titled Artificial Intelligence and the Law , warns that existing Australian common law, corporations law, and privacy statutes fail to keep pace with algorithmic deployment in corporate boardrooms and professional services.
